Au XVIIIe siècle, le royaume luba domine: In the 18th century, the Luba kingdom dominated the north of Shaba, in the Congo. Its court historians, the "men of memory", recited king lists and the epic of Mbidi Kiluwe and his son Kalala Ilunga while running a finger over a lukasa, a wooden board covered with beads. Their origin cannot be dated, but their place in the Bambudye society suggests they are very old.
Une planche de perles retient trois sièc: A board of beads holds three centuries of kings. You forget three of yesterday's questions.
Vers 556 av. J.-C., Simonide naît à Ioul: Around 556 BC, Simonides was born at Ioulis, on the island of Ceos. A poet in great demand, he is said to be the first to have charged for his verses. A legend, told by Cicero and then Quintilian, makes him the inventor of the art of memory: sole survivor of a banquet whose roof collapsed, he named each victim from their place at the table.
Simonide retrouvait les morts par leur p: Simonides found the dead by their places. I find your mistakes by their dates.
Vers 370 av. J.-C., Platon écrit le Phèd: Around 370 BC, Plato wrote the Phaedrus. Outside Athens, under a plane tree, Socrates tells how the god Theuth offered writing to Thamus, king of Egypt. The king refused the gift: writing would be a remedy for reminding, not for remembering, and would give the appearance of wisdom without wisdom. Socrates wrote nothing; Plato wrote everything.
Platon trouvait que l'écriture rend pare: Plato thought writing makes people lazy. He had not seen your revision cards.
Vers 90 av. J.-C., un auteur romain rest: Around 90 BC, a Roman author who remains unknown addressed a handbook of eloquence to a certain Gaius Herennius. It contains the first known description of the method of loci: placing striking images along a well-known route. The book, long attributed to Cicero, became the most read rhetoric handbook of the Middle Ages and the Renaissance; more than a hundred manuscripts survive.
Une méthode vieille de deux mille ans, q: A two-thousand-year-old method you have never tried. You are late, but consistent.
Metrodorus of Scepsis, born around 145 BC, a friend of King Mithridates VI of Pontus, was reputed to have the most prodigious memory of his time. He is said to have stored his memories in 360 places spread over the twelve signs of the zodiac. Around 70 BC, he died on the road, on the king's orders or of illness, according to Strabo.
Métrodore rangeait le monde dans le ciel: Metrodorus stored the world in the sky. You store your right answers nowhere.
Entre 1125 et 1130, à l'abbaye de Saint-: Between 1125 and 1130, at the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, the master Hugh wrote three treatises on Noah's ark. For his students, he advocated a rigid order, easy to remember, with a clear beginning, and sorted all knowledge into three philosophies, theoretical, practical and mechanical. For him, memory is no fairground trick: it is a discipline of the mind.
Hugues rangeait le savoir dans une arche: Hugh stored knowledge in an ark. You store it in a drawer you never open.
En 1263, à Majorque, Raymond Lulle voit: In 1263, in Majorca, Ramon Llull saw Christ on the cross. He then devoted his life to a universal Art: principles noted by letters, from B to R, which figures and circles combine with one another. Written in Catalan as much as in Latin, this Art would inspire Leibniz, and Giordano Bruno would blend it with the art of memory.
Lulle faisait tourner des roues pour com: Llull turned wheels to combine ideas. You just go round in circles.
En 1491, à Venise, le juriste Pierre de: In 1491, in Venice, the jurist Peter of Ravenna published Phoenix seu artificiosa memoria, the art of artificial memory. He boasted of having learned the whole civil code at ten. The book became one of the most popular memory treatises of the Renaissance, reprinted and translated, into English around 1548.
Pierre de Ravenne savait le code civil à: Peter of Ravenna knew the civil code at ten. At ten, you knew where the snacks were.
En 1634, à Paris, le mathématicien Pierr: In 1634, in Paris, the mathematician Pierre Hérigone published the first volume of his Cursus mathematicus, in French and Latin. In it he proposed remembering long numbers by giving each digit a consonant sound, the reader adding the vowels. Two centuries later, Aimé Paris would derive the modern major system from it.
Hérigone transformait les chiffres en mo: Hérigone turned digits into words. You turn words into mush.
En 1959, aux États-Unis, Lloyd et Margar: In 1959, in the United States, Lloyd and Margaret Peterson showed 24 students three consonants, such as TGH, then had them count backwards. After 3 seconds, they recalled about 80%; after 18 seconds, less than 10%. Short-term memory, deprived of rehearsal, fades in a few seconds.
Dix-huit secondes de mémoire. Je compren: Eighteen seconds of memory. Now I understand why you reread the question.
En 1972, en Allemagne, le journaliste sc: In 1972, in Germany, the science journalist Sebastian Leitner published So lernt man lernen. In it he described a card box with ever wider compartments, 1, 2, 5, 8 and 14 cm: a card answered correctly moves forward, a missed card goes back to the start. A simple way to review just what you forget, at the right time.
Leitner renvoyait les fiches ratées à la: Leitner sent missed cards back to the start. I do the same with you, on the board.
Le 13 avril 1929, d'après son journal, l: On 13 April 1929, according to his diary, the journalist Solomon Shereshevsky met the neuropsychologist Alexander Luria in Moscow. He retained entire lists, every sound gave him colours, every number a personality. Luria would study him for years and draw from it, in 1968, a famous book.
Cherechevski n'arrivait pas à oublier. V: Shereshevsky could not forget. You cannot remember. Nature is badly designed.
Le 1er septembre 1953, à l'hôpital de Ha: On 1 September 1953, at Hartford Hospital, in the United States, the neurosurgeon William Scoville operated on Henry Molaison, 27, an epileptic. He removed both hippocampi. The seizures decreased, but Henry could no longer form new memories. Studied for decades under the initials H. M., he revealed that memory is made of several systems.
H. M. oubliait tout ce qui était neuf. V: H. M. forgot everything new. You found a way to do it without surgery.
En 1956, le psychologue George Miller, d: In 1956, the psychologist George Miller, of Harvard, published in Psychological Review an article whose title became famous: "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two". Our immediate memory holds about seven chunks, whatever their size. It is one of the most cited articles in psychology.
Sept éléments en mémoire. Chez vous, j'e: Seven items in memory. In you, I count two, and one of them is my name.
En 1972, Fergus Craik et Robert Lockhart: In 1972, Fergus Craik and Robert Lockhart published "Levels of processing: A framework for memory research". Their idea: it is not the time spent that makes you remember, but the depth of processing. A word whose shape you looked at is quickly forgotten; a word whose meaning you sought stays.
Craik et Lockhart prouvent qu'il faut ré: Craik and Lockhart prove you have to think to remember. Now I understand your problem.
En 1975, Godden et Baddeley font écouter: In 1975, Godden and Baddeley had divers listen to 36 words, on the beach or underwater, then tested them in one setting or the other. Words learned underwater came back better underwater, beach words on the beach: the place is part of the memory.
Des plongeurs retiennent mieux sous l'ea: Divers remember better underwater. I suggest you revise at the bottom of a lake. Without an air tank.
En 2006, à l'université Washington de Sa: In 2006, at Washington University in St. Louis, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke had students study a passage. Some reread it again and again, the others tested themselves. Five minutes later, the rereaders won; a week later, the tested students retained 61% of the passage against 40%. Testing yourself is not just measuring: it is learning.
Se tester fait retenir. Je vous teste de: Testing makes you remember. I have been testing you for weeks. Thank me instead of sighing.
En 1991, à Londres, Tony Buzan et Ray Ke: In 1991, in London, Tony Buzan and Ray Keene organised the first World Memory Championship. Dominic O'Brien, who had been training for four years with places and characters, won it. He would win eight. Since then, the competition has been held every year, with one exception, 1992.
Des gens s'entraînent pour retenir un je: People train to memorise a deck of cards in thirteen seconds. You forget which suit is trumps.
En 2000, à Londres, la neuroscientifique: In 2000, in London, the neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire scanned the brains of 16 taxi drivers, who had learned the city map in about two years. The back of their hippocampus was larger than in 50 other men, all the more so the longer they had been driving. The adult brain reshapes itself as it learns.
Les taxis de Londres ont un hippocampe m: London taxi drivers have a muscular hippocampus. Yours is on sick leave.
En 1924, aux États-Unis, John Jenkins et: In 1924, in the United States, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach put to the test Ebbinghaus's theory that memories fade with time. Their results: after a period of sleep, people remember much better than after the same time spent awake. It is not only time that makes us forget, it is what we do during that time.
Dormir aide à retenir. Enfin une méthode: Sleep helps you remember. Finally a method that suits you.
